title: One Sport and Its Paper: Ice Hockey
bigQuestion: What can the written record of one sport, from a newspaper notice to a league charter, show about who was let in and who was kept out?

story.title: A Notice in the Morning Paper
story.kicker: In March 1875 a Montreal newspaper told readers about a game on indoor ice, and a paper trail began.
paragraphs: On March 3, 1875, the Montreal Gazette told its readers about a game to be played that evening at the Victoria Skating Rink. The rink was an indoor building with a sheet of natural ice. A young engineer named James Creighton had gathered two teams of nine players each. Skaters in Montreal already knew stick games on frozen rivers and ponds.

The notice promised that spectators could watch in safety. The players would use a flat wooden disc instead of a ball, so it would not fly into the crowd. The next day the paper reported on the game. Historians still read that report closely, because it is one of the earliest printed accounts of an organized game of hockey indoors.

Over the next fifty years the paper stack grew. Montreal clubs printed a short set of rules in 1877. A governor general bought a silver bowl in 1892 and wrote conditions for winning it. Owners met in a Montreal hotel in 1917 and founded a new league. Each document added a rule, a trophy or a membership list.

Each paper also answered a quiet question: who may play here? For decades the answer on most rosters was white men and boys. Black players in Nova Scotia formed their own league, women organized their own teams, and the paper record shows when those doors opened.
story.think: Why might a historian trust a newspaper notice from 1875 more than a story told a hundred years later?

lessons.title: Stick Games on Frozen Water
lessons.mainIdea: People played stick-and-ball games on ice in Europe and North America long before anyone wrote down hockey's rules.
reading: Dutch painters of the early 1600s left some of the oldest pictures of games on ice. Hendrick Avercamp painted crowded winter scenes on frozen canals. In several of them, people swing curved sticks at a ball. The Dutch game was called *kolf*, and it was also played on land. The paintings show a pastime, not a league, with no fixed teams or lines.

In Britain and Ireland, people played field games with sticks and a ball under names such as bandy, shinty and hurling. When British soldiers and settlers came to Canada, they carried these games onto frozen rivers and lakes. On the ice, the games had no agreed size of team and no written rules. Each town and garrison played its own way.

The Mi'kmaq people of Nova Scotia played a stick-and-ball game of their own. In the 1800s, Mi'kmaq carvers made many of the hardwood hockey sticks sold in Canada, often from hornbeam trees. Their sticks were shipped to clubs across the country. This trade connects the sport's early equipment to Indigenous craft workers, whose names seldom appear in club records.

words.d: a Dutch stick-and-ball game of the 1600s, played on ice and on land
a stick-and-ball game on ice played in Britain and northern Europe
an Indigenous nation of Canada's Atlantic coast whose carvers made many early hockey sticks

lessons.title: Birthplace Claims and Evidence
lessons.mainIdea: Several towns claim to be the birthplace of hockey, but historians separate those legends from the earliest printed records.
reading: Windsor, Nova Scotia, says that boys at King's College School played hockey on a pond in the early 1800s. The town points to a passage in the writings of Thomas Chandler Haliburton, a Nova Scotia author who attended that school. Kingston, Ontario, and Montreal have made their own claims. Each town has a museum, a plaque or a local story to support it.

A *birthplace claim* is a statement that a sport began in one place. Such claims help towns attract visitors and take pride in a game. Historians ask a harder question: what written record, made at the time, shows the game being played? A memory written down decades later is weaker evidence than a newspaper printed the next morning.

By that test, the Montreal game of March 3, 1875, stands out. It was announced ahead of time and described afterward in print. That does not mean nobody played hockey earlier. It means 1875 is the earliest date that historians can tie to a public, organized indoor game with a *primary source* behind it.

words.d: a statement that a sport began in one particular town or place
a record made at the time of an event, such as a newspaper report printed the next day
a traditional story that is told as history but cannot be proven by records from the time

look.prompt: Which piece of evidence is stronger for dating an organized game, and why might a town still value the other one?

choices: It is the proven first time anyone played hockey

check.why: The Montreal game was announced and reported in print, giving it strong evidence.

lessons.title: The Victoria Rink, 1875
lessons.mainIdea: An indoor rink in Montreal gave hockey a fixed room, a crowd and a newspaper audience in 1875.
reading: The Victoria Skating Rink opened in Montreal in 1862. It was a long brick building with a roof over natural ice. Members paid to skate there, and the rink held carnivals and costume balls. A roof meant the ice was protected from snow, and the walls marked the edges of the playing space.

On March 3, 1875, James Creighton brought two teams of nine players to the rink. Creighton had grown up in Halifax, Nova Scotia, and moved to Montreal as a young man. The players used a flat wooden *disc* instead of a ball. The Montreal Gazette said this choice would keep the object on the ice and protect the people watching.

The rink changed what hockey could become. A game in a building could be scheduled, advertised and watched by paying spectators. In 1883 Montreal's Winter Carnival held a hockey tournament, and in 1886 clubs formed the Amateur Hockey Association of Canada. A room, a crowd and a *club* came together, and written rules soon followed.

words.d: a building or space with a sheet of ice set aside for skating and games
the flat wooden object used in place of a ball at the 1875 game, an early form of the puck
a group of members who organize games and pay for a place to play
a body of hockey clubs formed in 1886 to run games under shared rules

check.why: The clubs formed the association in 1886, three years after the 1883 Winter Carnival tournament.

sections.title: Rules, a Trophy and a League

lessons.title: The Montreal Rules, 1877
lessons.mainIdea: In 1877 Montreal players printed a short set of hockey rules in the newspaper, borrowing from older field games.
reading: In February 1877 the Montreal Gazette printed seven rules for hockey. Students and club members in the city had drawn them up. Several rules were adapted from field hockey and rugby, which the players already knew. Printing the rules in a newspaper meant that anyone in Montreal could read the same text.

A written *code* lets strangers play together. Before 1877, a team from one town might argue with another about what was allowed. After the rules were printed, a captain could point to a sentence in the paper. McGill University students formed a hockey club in 1877, and they played under the new text.

The rules kept changing for decades. Team size fell from nine to seven by the 1880s, and later to six. Leagues added a *referee* to enforce the rules and a goal judge to rule on scores. Each change was voted on and printed, so historians can date many of them.

words.d: a written set of rules that players agree to follow
the official who enforces the rules during a game
the short set of hockey rules printed in the Montreal Gazette in 1877

look.prompt: Why does a printed rule settle the argument more easily than a town custom?

lessons.title: Lord Stanley's Bowl
lessons.mainIdea: The Stanley Cup began in 1892 as a governor general's challenge trophy for amateur clubs and later became the prize of one professional league.
reading: Frederick Arthur Stanley, Lord Stanley of Preston, was Canada's governor general from 1888 to 1893. His children played hockey in Ottawa, and his daughter Isobel was photographed on the ice around 1890. In 1892 Lord Stanley bought a silver bowl in London. He gave it as a *challenge trophy* for Canada's best amateur hockey club.

Stanley named two *trustees* to hold the bowl and settle disputes. The champion club had to accept challenges from other clubs that qualified. The Montreal Hockey Club, part of the Montreal Amateur Athletic Association, was named the first holder in 1893. Stanley went home to England that year and never saw a Cup game.

Over time, professional teams took over. The Seattle Metropolitans of the Pacific Coast league became the first American team to win the Cup, in 1917. By 1926 only National Hockey League teams played for it. Winners' names are engraved on bands added to the base, so the object itself became a record.

words.d: a prize that the holder must defend against qualified challengers, rather than win in a fixed season
a person named to hold property and make decisions about it for a stated purpose
the British Crown's representative in Canada
the silver trophy Lord Stanley gave in 1892, later the championship prize of the National Hockey League

look.title: Names on the Bands
look.text: The Stanley Cup's base is made of silver bands, each covered with engraved names of players, coaches and staff from winning teams. When the bands fill up, the oldest band is removed and kept at the Hockey Hall of Fame in Toronto, and a new blank band is added.
look.prompt: How is the Stanley Cup itself a historical record, and what happens to the oldest part of that record?

choices: A challenge trophy for amateur clubs
check.why: Lord Stanley gave it in 1892 as a challenge trophy for Canada's top amateur club.

check.why: The Montreal Hockey Club of the Montreal AAA was the first holder in 1893.

check.q: Which was the first American team to win the Stanley Cup?
check.why: The Seattle Metropolitans won the Cup in 1917.

lessons.title: A New League in a Hotel
lessons.mainIdea: The National Hockey League was founded in a Montreal hotel in 1917, partly to shut one owner out of the old league.
reading: By the early 1900s, hockey players could be paid openly. The International Professional Hockey League, based in Michigan's Upper Peninsula and nearby towns, played from 1904 to 1907. In Canada the National Hockey Association began in 1909. Its owners quarreled often, especially with Eddie Livingstone, who owned a Toronto club.

On November 26, 1917, several owners met at the Windsor Hotel in Montreal. Instead of expelling Livingstone, they formed a new league without him: the National Hockey League. The first NHL season had four clubs, and one, the Montreal Wanderers, dropped out after its arena burned in January 1918. The league's founding shows that a *charter* can be written to exclude as well as to organize.

The NHL grew in the 1920s by selling *franchises*, the rights to own a team in a city. The Boston Bruins joined in 1924 as the first American club. In 1926 the Chicago Black Hawks, the Detroit club and the New York Rangers joined. The Black Hawks, owned by Frederic McLaughlin, won their first Stanley Cup in 1934.

words.d: a founding document that sets up an organization and says who belongs
the right, sold by a league, to own and run a team in a city
the professional league founded in Montreal on November 26, 1917
paid openly to play a sport

lessons.title: A Black League in Nova Scotia
lessons.mainIdea: Black players in Nova Scotia built their own hockey league in 1895, decades before the NHL had a Black player.
reading: Black communities in Nova Scotia date back to the late 1700s, when Black Loyalists arrived after the American Revolution. In Halifax and nearby towns, Black churches were centers of community life. In 1895, Black players and community leaders formed the Colored Hockey League of the Maritimes. Its teams came from towns around Halifax and Dartmouth.

The league played for decades, drawing crowds to games on outdoor and rink ice. White clubs and associations did not admit these teams, so the league created its own schedule and championships. Historians George and Darril Fosty told its story in their 2004 book *Black Ice*. Much of what is known comes from old newspapers and family memories gathered in that research.

The NHL's first Black player came much later. Willie O'Ree of Fredericton, New Brunswick, first played for the Boston Bruins in 1958. The gap between 1895 and 1958 shows that an unwritten *color line* can shape a sport even when no rule names race. The Colored Hockey League is one of the institutions that kept playing during those years.

words.w: Colored Hockey League of the Maritimes
words.d: a league of Black hockey teams founded in Nova Scotia in 1895
Black people who sided with Britain in the American Revolution and settled in Nova Scotia and other colonies
a barrier, often unwritten, that kept Black athletes out of white teams and leagues

lessons.title: Women on the Ice
lessons.mainIdea: Women played hockey from the 1890s, but world championships, Olympic events and college titles for women came only from 1990 on.
reading: Around 1890, Isobel Stanley, the governor general's daughter, was photographed playing hockey outdoors in Ottawa. By the 1890s, women's teams played at Canadian universities and in towns. They often played in long skirts. In the 1930s, the Preston Rivulettes of Ontario won many Canadian women's titles.

International bodies were slow to add women. The International Ice Hockey Federation held its first Women's World Championship in Ottawa in 1990, and Canada won. Women's hockey joined the Olympic program at Nagano, Japan, in 1998. The United States won that first Olympic gold medal, beating Canada in the final.

In American colleges, *Title IX* of 1972 pushed schools to add women's teams. The NCAA held its first national championship in women's ice hockey in 2001, won by the University of Minnesota Duluth. In 1992 goalie Manon Rhéaume played in an NHL preseason game for the Tampa Bay Lightning, the first woman to do so.

words.d: the 1972 federal law that bars sex discrimination in education programs that receive federal money, including school sports
the world governing body of ice hockey, founded in Paris in 1908
the games played before a league's regular season begins

sections.title: A World Game with Written Rules

lessons.title: Paris, 1908, and the Olympics
lessons.mainIdea: European nations founded an international hockey federation in 1908, and hockey entered the Olympic Games in 1920.
reading: On May 15, 1908, delegates met in Paris and founded the Ligue Internationale de Hockey sur Glace. Today it is called the International Ice Hockey Federation. Its first members were European, including France, Belgium, Switzerland, Great Britain and Bohemia. Canada and the United States joined in 1920.

Ice hockey first appeared at the Olympics in 1920 at Antwerp, Belgium, during the Summer Games. Canada sent the Winnipeg Falcons, a club made up mostly of players from Icelandic immigrant families. The Falcons won the gold medal. When the first Winter Olympics were held at Chamonix, France, in 1924, hockey moved there.

International hockey needed a shared rule book, because North American and European rinks and rules differed. The *federation* wrote rules for its tournaments. For decades the Olympics admitted only *amateurs*, so NHL players stayed home. NHL players first took part in the Olympic tournament in 1998.

words.d: a body that joins national associations and writes rules for international play
a player who is not paid to play; the Olympics long admitted only amateurs
the Canadian club that won the first Olympic hockey gold medal in 1920

look.title: Two Rinks, Two Rule Books
look.text: In the early 1900s, a Canadian team used to its own rinks and rules traveled to play in Europe. The ice surface was a different size, and some rules on passing and substitutions were not the same. Officials from each side had learned different books.
look.prompt: Why would an international federation need its own rule book before nations could hold championships?

check.why: Delegates founded the Ligue Internationale de Hockey sur Glace in Paris on May 15, 1908.

check.why: Hockey was played at the 1920 Summer Games in Antwerp, then moved to the Winter Games in 1924.

check.q: When did NHL players first play in the Olympic tournament?
check.why: Because the Olympics long admitted only amateurs, NHL players first took part in 1998.

lessons.title: Injuries and the Rule Book
lessons.mainIdea: A goalie's mask in 1959 and a player's death in 1968 pushed hockey toward rules requiring head protection.
reading: For decades most NHL goalies played without masks. On November 1, 1959, Montreal Canadiens goalie Jacques Plante was cut in the face by a shot during a game in New York. He returned wearing a mask he had made for practice. His coach had resisted, but Plante kept wearing it, and masks slowly became normal for goalies.

On January 13, 1968, Bill Masterton of the Minnesota North Stars hit his head on the ice during a game, and he died two days later. He was the first NHL player to die from an injury suffered in a game. The league later named a trophy for him. His death led many to call for *helmets*, but the league did not require them at once.

In 1979 the NHL adopted a rule that players entering the league after that year must wear helmets. Players already in the league could choose, under a *grandfather clause*. The last player to play without a helmet, Craig MacTavish, retired in 1997. The rule shows how leagues often change slowly, protecting new players while exempting veterans.

words.d: a hard hat worn to protect the head from injury
a rule that exempts people already in a group from a new requirement
an NHL award named for Bill Masterton, who died after a game injury in 1968
